prompt.context: Your client, ABBS (Always Be Being Skiing) Resorts, is the #2 ski resort collective in the US, with multiple ski resorts throughout the country. They are looking to acquire another ski resort in the US.
prompt.question: What should ABBS consider when evaluating a potential acquisition target?

clarifying_info.q: What is ABBS's primary objective for the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: ABBS is most concerned with choosing a target that makes strategic sense (market share, ROI, growth outlook, competition, culture fit, strategic locations, etc.). Investors are very demanding and it must be a profitable investment within a 5-year window.

clarifying_info.q: Does ABBS already have specific targets in mind?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, ABBS has some targets in mind; we will get into that later.
The #1 player is Bean Resorts with 40% market share. Bean has been aggressively acquiring resorts and stealing share. ABBS currently holds 20% market share.
Both ABBS and Bean Resorts are based in Utah, but own multiple mountains throughout the country.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the US ski industry?
clarifying_info.a: The US ski industry is $5B, with 20 million total skiers (defined as snowsports participants including snowboarders).

exhibits.title: Acquisition Target Regions
exhibits.shows: A map of four target states/regions (Oregon, Utah, Montana, New England) showing the locations of ABBS properties, Bean Resorts properties, and independent (target) properties within those regions only.
exhibits.data: Three legend categories: ABBS property, Bean Resorts property, Target (independent) property. Only mountains in target regions are shown.

exhibits.title: Regional Metrics
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis chart with annual ski visits (millions) on the left axis and projected CAGR (%) on the right axis for four regions: Utah, Oregon, New England, and Montana.
exhibits.data: Utah: ~25M annual visits, low CAGR (~0%); Oregon: ~20M annual visits, low CAGR; New England: ~10M annual visits, high CAGR (~30%); Montana: ~10M annual visits, moderate CAGR.

exhibits.title: Skier Demographic Data
exhibits.shows: Two panels: (1) stacked bar chart of skier demographic mix by region (Beginners, PATs, Luxury, Casual/Millennials as % of visits); (2) a bubble chart plotting spend per visit vs. projected CAGR by segment, with bubble size representing relative demographic size.
exhibits.data: Oregon: ~10% Beginners, ~55% PATs, ~30% Luxury, ~5% Millennials. Montana: ~20% Beginners, ~35% PATs, ~40% Luxury, ~5% Millennials. New England: ~30% Beginners, ~15% PATs, ~10% Luxury, ~45% Millennials. Utah: ~5% Beginners, ~35% PATs, ~25% Luxury, ~35% Millennials. Segment CAGR: PATs=flat, Beginners=+, Millennials=+, Luxury=-. Spend per visit: Luxury=high, Millennials=moderate-high, Beginners=moderate, PATs=low.

exhibits.title: Contribution Margin by Segment (Owl's Peak)
exhibits.shows: A table/chart for Owl's Peak showing contribution margin per visit by segment, total annual contribution margin for some segments, and the customer segment mix (pie chart). A footnote notes that 10% of total annual contribution margin will come from existing ABBS customers choosing Owl's Peak instead (cannibalization).
exhibits.data: Beginners: $100 contribution margin/visit; Millennials: $250 contribution margin/visit; PATs: $12.5M total annual contribution margin (cell pre-filled); Luxury: segment present. Owl's Peak customer segment mix: Beginners 33%, Millennials 50% (remaining split between PATs and Luxury). Footnote: 10% of total annual CM = cannibalization from existing ABBS customers.

exhibits.title: Two Improvement Options for Owl's Peak
exhibits.shows: A summary card describing two options ABBS is evaluating to improve the investment case for Owl's Peak.
exhibits.data: Option 1 (Eliminate PATs): Marketing campaign to attract 33% more millennials; for every extra millennial visit one PAT visit is eliminated; Cost=$0; implemented immediately; eliminates cannibalization. Option 2 (Food ordering app): SkiGrub app allowing food orders on the mountain; brand new technology; Cost=$5M; implemented immediately; eliminates cannibalization; increases food contribution margin by 20%.

framework: Acquirer analysis: geographic locations, existing strengths, financial position, current market share and demographics

Target evaluation: potential synergies (cross-selling, multi-mountain ski pass, unified brand marketing, new innovations, cost reductions) and risks (culture clash, market saturation, low-growth demographics/geographies, cannibalization of existing ABBS resorts)
Market assessment: overall ski industry growth, changing demographics (especially millennials), customer loyalty to Bean Resorts, macro risks such as global warming
Financial viability: target price, expected revenue/contribution margin, 5-year breakeven requirement set by investors
Competitive positioning: impact on market share relative to Bean Resorts, strategic location value

questions.prompt: Evaluate the four target regions (Oregon, Utah, Montana, New England) using Exhibits 1a, 1b, and 1c. Which region is most attractive?
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize insights from all three exhibits, ideally in a comparison table. Key conclusions: New England has the least competition (Exhibit 1a), the fastest CAGR despite smallest current size (Exhibit 1b — at 30% CAGR it surpasses Utah in ~3 years), and the best demographic mix (high Millennials and Beginners — both high-margin, high-growth; Exhibit 1c). Utah and Montana are saturated or PAT/Luxury-heavy (flat/negative growth demographics). Oregon has no competitor presence but ABBS already has resorts there. Strong candidate synthesizes with a scored table and recommends New England.

math.setup: New England CAGR math: NE starts ~10M visits growing at ~30% CAGR vs Utah ~25M at ~0%. Years to surpass: 10*(1.3)^n > 25 → (1.3)^n > 2.5 → n ≈ 3.5 years (rough calculation).
math.answer: New England surpasses Utah in approximately 3 years at 30% CAGR, confirming it as the highest-growth region.

questions.prompt: ABBS is considering buying Owl's Peak (Vermont) for $1.3B. Calculate the total annual contribution margin at Owl's Peak and determine whether this meets the 5-year breakeven requirement.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that revenue flows from multiple streams (tickets, food, rentals, lessons, merchandise) and that these are wrapped into contribution margin per visit. Needs to determine total visits from Exhibit 1b (Owl's Peak = 10% of NE total), then multiply by segment mix and CM/visit from Exhibit 2. Must apply 10% cannibalization discount. Conclusion: does NOT meet 5-year breakeven.

math.setup: Total NE ski visits from Exhibit 1b = ~15M (10M shown, but use ~15M per casebook). Owl's Peak = 10% of NE total = 1.5M visits. Segment mix from Exhibit 2: Beginners 33%, Millennials 50%, remainder to PATs/Luxury. CM/visit: Beginners=$100, Millennials=$250, PATs=$50 (derived: $12.5M total / 250k visits). Cannibalization = 10% discount on total CM.
steps: Breakeven: $1.3B / $225M ≈ 5.8 years > 5 years → does NOT meet requirement
math.answer: Net annual contribution margin ≈ $225M. Breakeven ≈ 5.8 years, which exceeds the 5-year investor requirement. The investment is NOT worthwhile as-is.

questions.prompt: (Exhibit 2 guidance) What is the PAT contribution margin per visit?
questions.guidance: This is a derived number. Total PAT CM is given as $12.5M. PAT visits = 250k (residual after Beginners and Millennials). $12.5M / 250k = $50/visit. Useful for Option 1 math.

math.setup: PAT CM/visit = Total PAT CM / PAT visits

questions.prompt: Option 1: A marketing campaign increases millennial visits by 33% at the expense of PAT visits, at zero cost and eliminates cannibalization. Does this make the investment worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the new contribution margin after shifting visits from PATs to Millennials. Strong candidates will also flag PR, cultural, and community risks of eliminating the PAT segment.

math.setup: 33% of 750k millennial visits = 250k new millennial visits, which exactly replaces all 250k PAT visits. New CM replaces PAT CM with higher-margin Millennial CM. Cannibalization eliminated.
steps: CM gain per visit swap: $250 (millennial) - $50 (PAT) = $200 difference
math.answer: New annual CM = $300M. Breakeven ≈ 4.3 years. Option 1 WORKS financially, but carries risk of alienating PAT community and potential PR backlash.

questions.prompt: Option 2: The SkiGrub food ordering app increases food contribution margin by 20% across all segments and costs $5M (unproven technology). Does this make the investment worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the technology risk (brand new, unproven) and calculate the incremental CM from food improvement across each segment. Food = 50% of average CM per visit across segments.

math.setup: Food revenue = 50% of average CM per visit for each segment. 20% improvement on food portion. Cost = $5M one-time.
steps: Beginners: food CM/visit = 50% * $100 = $50; increase = 20% * $50 = $10/visit; 500k visits * $10 = $5M additional
Millennials: food CM/visit = 50% * $250 = $125; increase = 20% * $125 = $25/visit; 750k visits * $25 = $18.75M additional
PATs: food CM/visit = 50% * $50 = $25; increase = 20% * $25 = $5/visit; 250k visits * $5 = $1.25M additional
Net CM increase after app cost: $25M - $5M = $20M
math.answer: New annual CM = $270M. Breakeven ≈ 4.8 years. Option 2 works financially but carries technology risk since SkiGrub is unproven.

brainstorming.prompt: ABBS seeks to differentiate by offering unique, world-class skiing experiences. What are ways ABBS can improve the overall experience for someone considering skiing at Owl's Peak?

categories.name: Planning & Purchasing
ideas: Dynamic ticket pricing and bundling options
Online purchasing with add-ons (lessons, rentals, lockers)
Multi-day/multi-mountain pass packages
Loyalty program integration

categories.name: Transportation to Mountain
ideas: Valet parking or shuttle services
Real-time weather and road condition updates via app
Partnerships with rideshare companies
Designated ski gear transport/storage for commuters

categories.name: Pre-Mountain Experience
ideas: Streamlined equipment rental shops with reservation system
Self-service ticket kiosks to eliminate lines
Daycare and family services
VR preview of mountain conditions and runs
Interactive mountain trail maps at base

categories.name: On-Mountain Experience
ideas: Faster, heated chairlifts
Mountain-wide WiFi
Mobile food ordering (e.g., SkiGrub app)
Equipment valet at mid-mountain
Improved trail grooming and signage
Dedicated beginner zones with instructor availability
Indoor/simulator skiing for non-ski days or bad weather
Live entertainment or music at key lift areas

categories.name: Post-Mountain / Après Ski
ideas: Curated après ski events, nightlife, and entertainment
High-quality food & beverage options at the lodge
Babysitting and family programming
Loyalty engagement: push notifications, personalized offers
Community events to build brand affinity (especially for Millennials)

recommendation: ABBS should target a resort in New England due to its superior growth trajectory (fastest CAGR, will surpass Utah in ~3 years), favorable demographics (high Millennial and Beginner mix — both high-margin and growing), and lack of meaningful competitor presence

Regarding Owl's Peak specifically: as-is the investment does not meet the 5-year breakeven at $225M annual CM. ABBS should either (a) pursue Option 1 (millennial marketing campaign) which yields $300M CM and 4.3-year breakeven, or (b) pursue Option 2 (SkiGrub app) which yields $270M CM and 4.8-year breakeven. Option 1 is financially stronger but carries cultural/PR risk; Option 2 is safer culturally but relies on unproven technology. Alternatively, ABBS could seek a different New England mountain with a more favorable entry price.
risks: Option 1 eliminates the PAT segment entirely, risking community backlash, negative PR, and loss of a loyal customer base that may also influence others
Option 2 depends on unproven technology; if SkiGrub fails to deliver, the incremental CM does not materialize and breakeven slips beyond 5 years
Cannibalization risk: even after elimination adjustments, some customer overlap with existing ABBS properties may persist
Macro risk: global warming poses long-term threat to ski industry viability, particularly for lower-elevation resorts
Bean Resorts (40% market share) has a head start in aggressive acquisitions and may outbid or pre-empt ABBS in New England
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on Owl's Peak financials, infrastructure, and brand reputation
Assess feasibility and pilot results for SkiGrub technology before committing to Option 2
Model PAT segment cultural impact and develop a mitigation plan if pursuing Option 1
Explore other potential New England targets in case Owl's Peak valuation cannot be negotiated down
Develop multi-mountain pass strategy to leverage New England acquisition for cross-selling across ABBS portfolio
